status_summary: The recommendation's first element (federal charges and a larger federal presence) has been applied in two places, and DOJ has opened investigations of two local prosecutors' offices. In D.C., where the federal government has more direct authority, Executive Orders 14252 (signed 2025-03-27), 14333 (2025-08-11), 14339 and 14340 (both 2025-08-25) created a task force, delegated direction of Metropolitan Police services for federal purposes to the Attorney General, directed more federal prosecutors, and called for federal custody and charges for arrestees where possible. In Memphis, a presidential memorandum of 2025-09-15 created the Memphis Safe Task Force with the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Western District of Tennessee as a member; that office reported 195 defendants charged from 2025-10-01 to 2025-12-31 (its own figure), received 20 military lawyers as Special Assistant U.S. Attorneys on 2026-01-07, and announced five additional Assistant U.S. Attorneys on 2026-02-26 citing the rise in case filings. On the second element, DOJ's Civil Rights Division opened two investigations of local prosecutors' offices: one of the Hennepin County, Minnesota Attorney's Office announced on 2025-05-05 over a plea policy that allowed consideration of race, closed on 2026-02-26 after DOJ said the office had corrected the policy (the county disputed DOJ's authority and framing), and, announced on 2026-05-06, one of the Fairfax County, Virginia Commonwealth's Attorney's plea, charging and sentencing policies, framed in DOJ's release as a question of preferential treatment for defendants without lawful status under Title VI, the Safe Streets Act and 34 U.S.C. 12601, which the office calls lawful; DOJ's release states no conclusions had been reached and no finding was reported in the Fairfax matter. No DOJ lawsuit against a prosecutor for declining to prosecute was found, and the Attorney General's cash bail jurisdiction list under Executive Order 14342 (due about 2025-09-24) was not located.

timeline.event: Executive Order 14252 creates the D.C. Safe and Beautiful Task Force (members include the FBI, Marshals Service, ATF and the U.S. Attorney's offices for D.C., Maryland and Eastern Virginia), calls for a more robust federal law enforcement presence in parts of D.C., and directs a review of federal prosecutorial policies on pretrial detention (published 2025-04-03 at 90 FR 14559).

DOJ's Civil Rights Division announces an investigation of the Hennepin County, Minnesota Attorney's Office, citing public reporting that a county plea-negotiation policy directs prosecutors to weigh a defendant's racial identity; the release invokes the Constitution and federal civil rights laws without naming specific statutes and says the review will cover the office's policies and practices on the consideration of race. The office said it would cooperate and that its policy complies with the law (per the ABA Journal).

Executive Order 14333 declares a crime emergency in D.C. under section 740 of the Home Rule Act and delegates to the Attorney General the direction of Metropolitan Police services for federal purposes (published 2025-08-14 at 90 FR 39301).

Executive Order 14340 directs D.C. task force officials to hold arrestees in federal custody and pursue federal charges and pretrial detention where possible and directs the Attorney General to review Metropolitan Police orders on pretrial release; Executive Order 14339 the same day directs the U.S. Attorney for D.C. to hire more prosecutors for violent and property crime and calls for a specialized public-safety unit deployable in D.C. and possibly other cities; and Executive Order 14342 directs the Attorney General to deliver within 30 days a list of states and localities that have substantially eliminated cash bail for certain serious offenses, with agencies and OMB to identify federal funds to those jurisdictions that could be suspended or ended as the law permits (published 2025-08-28 at 90 FR 42125, 42121 and 42129). No published cash bail list was located.

A presidential memorandum, 'Restoring Law and Order in Memphis,' establishes the Memphis Safe Task Force, which includes the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Western District of Tennessee and federal law enforcement agencies, and directs a request to Tennessee's governor for National Guard support.

The U.S. Attorney's Office for the Western District of Tennessee announces that 20 military lawyers have been assigned as Special Assistant U.S. Attorneys to prosecute task force cases, and reports 195 defendants charged from 2025-10-01 to 2025-12-31, with 111 indictments charging 141 defendants versus 35 indictments charging 37 defendants in the same quarter of 2024 (the office's own figures; the release's breakdown of complaints and indictments does not sum cleanly to 195).

DOJ's Civil Rights Division closes its Hennepin County Attorney's Office review. The Assistant Attorney General's letter to the County Attorney, as reported by Bring Me The News, says the office has corrected a policy DOJ viewed as unconstitutional; no DOJ press release was found. On 2026-02-27 the Hennepin County Attorney's Office issued a statement saying DOJ never had authority to investigate, that its policy was constitutional, and that a policy update acknowledges racial disparities in the county's criminal legal system (the Thursday date comes from a local report published 2026-02-27).

DOJ's Civil Rights Division announces an investigation of the Fairfax County, Virginia Commonwealth's Attorney's plea bargaining, charging and sentencing policies, asking whether the office discriminated against U.S. citizens by giving preferential treatment to defendants without lawful status. The release cites Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, the Safe Streets Act and 34 U.S.C. 12601, states that DOJ has reached no conclusions, and says similar past investigations led to settlements with reforms. The office's spokesperson called the characterization a distortion and the office has described its policies as lawful (per Courthouse News). No subpoena, finding or lawsuit was reported in the sources read.

The U.S. Attorney's Office for D.C. task force page (last updated 2026-08-12 per the fetch) reports more than 16,000 arrests and nearly 2,000 firearms seized in the surge, without a stated date range (DOJ's own figures, not independently checked).

title: Bring federal charges and more federal presence where local prosecution is limited
uncertainties: The D.C. and Memphis figures are the U.S. Attorneys' own and were not independently checked; the 2026-01-07 Memphis release's counts (136 by complaint and 141 by indictment against 195 total) do not sum cleanly, and the D.C. page gives no date range. Searches did not find any federal surge, task force memorandum or Federal Register presidential document for cities other than D.C. and Memphis (a Federal Register query for presidential documents mentioning Memphis, cashless bail or law and order since 2025-09-01 found none beyond a Police Week proclamation), but news coverage of other deployments (for example Chicago, Portland, New Orleans, Minneapolis) was not reviewed beyond the Supreme Court's Illinois order, and those deployments are largely Guard or immigration enforcement operations rather than DOJ charging. The Hennepin and Fairfax investigations are the only DOJ actions found against local prosecutors' offices; they concern race-conscious or immigration-related plea and charging policy rather than a flat refusal to prosecute, so they match the Mandate's second bullet only in part, and the Hennepin release names no specific statute. A Daily Signal report places a House Judiciary Committee subpoena to the same prosecutor in mid-September 2026 (a congressional step, exact date not confirmed) and says the committee sent a document request to the Boulder, Colorado district attorney. A report in Sept 2026 that a federal judge referred the Philadelphia district attorney to federal prosecutors concerns a habeas case and a court's referral, not an administration policy, and was not treated as a match. The cash bail list was searched for in a Federal Register query and one news search without result; it may exist unpublished. Leadership of DOJ changed in 2026 (a trade page headline dated 2026-04-02 reports the removal of Attorney General Bondi), and the effect on these policies was not examined. Executive Orders 14252, 14333, 14339, 14340 and 14342 were re-fetched from the Federal Register in this pass.
